angle: The 3 buckets of signals: out-of-the-box, custom, and first-party
post_first_line: 3 signal buckets. That's how Cole Courson sorts everything.
linkedin_post:
3 signal buckets. That's how Cole Courson sorts everything.

There could be more, but Cole Courson says simplifying to three is what makes the whole thing usable.

Bucket 1 is out-of-the-box signals. Think of what Unify, Clay, Sixsense, and a number of other providers in the space give you: website intent tracking, persona-level tracking, champion tracking, new hires, and job changes. Flip the switch and you have them.

Cole Courson calls these interesting at layer 1, but more interesting once they're compounded.

Bucket 2 is custom signals. Technographics. Job scraping, like hiring for specific roles. Social listening on Reddit, GitHub, and maybe Glassdoor for pain points.

Cole Courson says these are really, really important to dive into.

The point: out-of-the-box signals get you started, and custom signals are where you go deeper.

Which bucket are you leaning on most today?

lesson.title: Simplify your signals into buckets
takeaways: Out-of-the-box signals like website intent, champion tracking, new hires, and job changes are available from several providers.
Out-of-the-box signals are interesting at layer 1 but become more interesting when compounded.
Custom signals like technographics, job scraping, and social listening on Reddit, GitHub, or Glassdoor are really important to dive into.
lesson.exercise: List every signal you currently use and label each one out-of-the-box or custom. Then pick one custom signal, like hiring for a specific role, to add.

angle: Two things Google flags in high-volume cold email, and how to avoid them
linkedin_post:
Cole Courson sends 400k emails monthly.

Google flags two things at that volume, and most senders miss the second one.

The first is sameness. Google looks at the variability from one email to the next. Cole Courson builds in small differences with dynamic snippets: first name, company name, and sender name, plus spintax. Each one makes the next email a little different from the last, which makes landing at scale far more effective.

The second is a subject line that disconnects from the body. If the subject says one thing and the message says another, Google can flag it as spam.

The fix for both is simple. Vary the details, and make sure the subject line actually matches what the email says.

Which one have you been missing in your campaigns?

Slide 2: First flag: emails that look identical from one send to the next.
Slide 3: Google looks at variability between one email and the next.
Slide 4: Drive variability with first name, company name, and sender name.
Slide 5: Add spintax snippets to vary the copy itself.
Slide 6: Second flag: a subject line that disconnects from the body.
Slide 7: If subject and message don't match, Google can flag it as spam.
Slide 8: Vary the details. Match the subject to the message.

lesson.title: Two things Google flags in high-volume cold email
takeaways: Google looks at variability from one email to the next, so identical sends at scale are a risk.
Dynamic snippets like first name, company name, sender name, and spintax create small differences that help you land at large scale.
A subject line that disconnects from the body of the message can be flagged as spam.
lesson.exercise: Pull up your last broad campaign. Count how many dynamic snippets it uses, add at least one more, then check that every subject line matches what its email body is actually about.

angle: Why one big send day can get your mailboxes cancelled and cost you a month of warmup
post_first_line: One email blast can cost you a month.
linkedin_post:
One email blast can cost you a month.

Cole Courson has seen what happens when sending volume suddenly spikes, and it's not pretty.

Picture a team sending 50 emails a day, every day, with steady volume. Then someone decides to blast a 100,000-person webinar list.

Google flags the break in that consistent send pattern. Mailboxes get cancelled and domains get shut down.

The damage goes beyond the blast itself. Those messages disappear, and the odds of landing in spam get worse.

Then comes the recovery. Warming up domains typically takes 2 to 3 weeks, so a single send day can leave you spending a month warming them back up.

Cole Courson has been through that process personally, and called it really, really painful.

The fix is to scale volume gradually instead of in one jump.

What's the biggest send spike you've ever seen?

lesson.title: Don't Spike Your Send Volume
takeaways: Google flags changes in consistent day-to-day send volume, like jumping from 50 a day to 100,000.
The penalty can include cancelled mailboxes and shut down domains.
Domain warmup typically takes 2 to 3 weeks, so recovery can cost a month.
lesson.exercise: Pull your daily send numbers for the last 30 days. Check for any jumps, then write a ramp plan that scales volume gradually before your next big campaign or webinar list.

angle: 'Saw you on our website' is lazy: give prospects a real reason to talk to you
post_first_line: Bobby Foose calls out "saw you on our website."
linkedin_post:
Bobby Foose calls out "saw you on our website."

It's the most common opener in outbound, and it says almost nothing.

Bobby's point: put yourself in the other person's shoes. Why would they want to talk to you? A very valid answer is that they don't.

So the job is to give them a reason that goes beyond "saw you on our website." That line is lazy, and it shows no homework at all.

A better version is personal. Bobby's example: "Hey, you're from the same hometown as me. Now based in San Francisco, working at a startup called Unify. Here's what we do."

That opener shows a real connection. It gives the reader something to respond to, and it shows someone actually looked.

The bar isn't a clever line. The bar is proof that homework happened at all.

What's the best opener you've ever received?

Slide 2: Put yourself in the other person's shoes first.
Slide 3: Why would they want to talk to you?
Slide 4: A valid answer: they don't.
Slide 5: So you have to give them a real reason.
Slide 6: "Saw you on our website" shows zero homework.
Slide 7: Try a real connection, like a shared hometown.
Slide 8: Then say who you are and what you do.

lesson.title: Give Prospects a Real Reason to Talk to You
takeaways: Assume the prospect has no inherent desire to talk to you, and write from that starting point.
"Saw you on our website" is lazy because it shows no homework.
A personal connection, like a shared hometown, gives the reader a reason to engage before you explain what you do.
lesson.exercise: Rewrite your last three outbound openers that lean on "saw you on your website." For each, find one real connection or detail about the person and lead with that instead.

angle: Stop obsessing over Gmail vs Outlook: org size and a single channel are the bigger deliverability problem
post_first_line: Cole Courson says email provider isn't the problem.
linkedin_post:
Cole Courson says email provider isn't the problem.

The real deliverability issue sits somewhere most teams aren't looking.

Cole Courson's take: best practices are still best practices, so get those right first. After that, org size matters more than Gmail vs Outlook.

Emailing into large organizations is just tougher. They have spam checkers and blockers. Sometimes they pay for platforms that don't let your emails through.

So worry more about those nuances than about which inbox your prospect uses.

That's where multichannel comes in. Get signals and intent, send a good email, then refer to that email in a cold call. That gives the rep a real shot at an opportunity.

Cole Courson pointed out that there are 3 channels. Even in an email course, the recommendation was to use all of them.

Where does your outreach stall most: inbox or channel mix?

lesson.title: Deliverability beyond the inbox provider
takeaways: Best practices come first, then worry about org size nuances.
Large organizations are tougher to email because of spam checkers, blockers, and paid platforms.
Multichannel lets a good email be referenced in a cold call, creating a better opportunity.
lesson.exercise: Pick one target account at a large organization. Plan an email using a signal or intent, then write the cold call opener that references that email.

angle: 300-400K emails a month run by one orchestrator, and why a case study like that belongs in your email framework
linkedin_post:
300-400K emails a month. One orchestrator.

That number belongs in your email framework, and most teams leave it out.

Cole Courson works with one point of contact at Guru, who sends about 300 to 400K emails a month. With one orchestrator and Cole Courson running it, the whole thing stays clean.

That saves time and energy, and it still drives marketing results. It also becomes a strong case study.

In an email framework, one of the core pieces is the story: what type of result have we helped someone get? A proof point like this is exactly what that slot is for.

But the story isn't where Cole Courson says to start. Before email one for founder-led sales, you need to know where you're starting.

That means the personas, the splits, some of the pains, and the stories.

Get those four right first. The emails get easier to write after that.

What story would you lead your first email with?

lesson.title: Build the story before you write email one
takeaways: A good email framework includes a story about who you've helped and what changed for them.
A case study like one orchestrator running about 300 to 400K emails a month shows time saved, energy saved, and marketing results still driven.
Before email one in founder-led sales, nail down personas, splits, pains, and stories.
lesson.exercise: Write down your personas, how you split them, the top pain for each, and one customer story per persona. Then draft email one.
